problem: Bennett's visit (March 1847) came before the Poor Law Extension Act (June 1847), so he cannot have found that 'the new Poor Law' failed. Also, only one letter (Nicholson to Bennett) is attested, not mutual correspondence among all three.

fix.note: Two Quakers and an American evangelical cover the same peninsula within months of each other, and Nicholson writes to Bennett for help. Bennett saw Erris before the Poor Law Extension Act; Tuke and Nicholson both found that the new Poor Law could not work there.

problem: Trevelyan was knighted (KCB) on 27 April 1848, which is spring, and his essay appeared in January. The wording 'that same summer' implies the knighthood came in summer.

fix.note: Trevelyan writes as if the crisis were finished and is knighted in April; that summer Kennedy, who works for the system Trevelyan built, is listing the families evicted in Clare.

problem: Government soup kitchens peaked in July 1847 (about 3 million rations a day) and were shut down from mid-August to September. In July they were not yet 'winding down'.

The Russians did not have 'about a month' of talks. Pallada waited at Nagasaki from August to late November 1853 without meeting plenipotentiaries, left for Shanghai, and returned in January 1854, when the talks with Kawaji actually took place.

fix.digest: Goncharov writes to friends in St Petersburg from Nagasaki, where the Russians would wait for months for Edo's envoys, sailing off to Shanghai in November and returning in January. His letters, later folded into Frigate 'Pallada', turn Japanese ceremony and evasion into comedy — and into a portrait of a closed society about to be pried open by others.
